###### *An easy-to-understand breakdown of the different banking codes needed for making international payments.*


How do you find a SWIFT code from an IBAN (and when do you need it)?


If you’re **sending international payments** , you’re no doubt familiar with the **various banking codes required** to ensure your payment reaches the recipient. You may well have also had occasions where you’ve entered the wrong digit and a payment never reached the beneficiary it was meant to reach.


For example, if you need a SWIFT code from an IBAN, many banks or payment platforms can look it up automatically, but sometimes you’ll need to confirm the SWIFT/BIC with the recipient or their bank.


In this guide, we break down the **most common banking codes** so you can understand what they mean, when you need them, and how to avoid mistakes.


## The most common banking codes used in international payments


In **most**[global payment](https://www.corpay.com/cross-border/global-payments) **scenarios,** businesses are asked to provide a combination of **banking identifiers** depending on the destination country, payment type, and currency.


### The three codes you’re most likely to need


-


**SWIFT/BIC** (the bank identifier for cross-border wire messaging)


-


**IBAN** (the account identifier used in many countries, especially across Europe and other IBAN-participating regions)


-


**Routing number** (ABA/RTN) (the U.S. domestic bank identifier used for ACH and often for wires)


Which one you **need depends on** the **destination country, payment type** (wire vs. local transfer), and **currency** .


**Beyond bank codes** , account setup can also affect how smoothly international payments are processed. Businesses that need to send and receive payments[in different currencies](https://www.corpay.com/cross-border/multi-currency-accounts) may **reduce unnecessary conversions** and use the most appropriate local or international payment details or international payment details.


## What is a SWIFT code (also known as BIC)?


A **SWIFT code** (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication), often called a **BIC** (Bank Identifier Code), is **used to identify a bank** (or financial institution) internationally. A BIC is 8 characters, and it can optionally include a 3-character branch code (making it 11 characters total).


### What a SWIFT/BIC looks like


A SWIFT/BIC code is typically structured like this:


-


**Bank/business party prefix** (4 letters/numbers)


-


**Country code** (2 letters, based on ISO country codes)


-


**Location code** (2 letters/numbers)


-


**Branch code** (optional, 3 letters/numbers)


#### Example: Barclays Bank SWIFT/BIC


**BUKBGB22 0KP**


-


BUKB = bank code


-


GB = country


-


22 = location


-


0KP = branch (optional)


That example matches the **standard format** , even though some elements are letters/numbers depending on the institution.


### Other codes often confused with SWIFT/BIC


SWIFT/BIC may sometimes be mentioned alongside CHIPS, NCC, BSC, or IFSC, but these are not equivalent identifiers.


-


**CHIPS** (Clearing House Interbank Payments System) is a U.S. clearing system for large-value USD payments. It’s a payment network, not a bank identifier.


-


**IFSC** (Indian Financial System Code) is a domestic bank identifier used in India.


-


**NCC** (National Clearing Code) refers to a country-specific bank or branch clearing code used within local payment systems.


-


**BSC** (Bank/Branch Sort Code) refers to domestic bank or branch codes (such as UK sort codes) used for local clearing.


-


**Bacs** (Bankers’ Automated Clearing Services) is a UK batch clearing system used for Direct Debit and Direct Credit payments. It supports low-cost domestic transfers and typically settles on a three-business-day cycle.


-


**CHAPS** (Clearing House Automated Payment System) is the UK’s high-value real-time gross settlement (RTGS) payment system for GBP transfers, providing same-day settlement and immediate finality.


These codes support domestic clearing or specific payment networks, whereas SWIFT/BIC is a distinct international bank identifier standard.


#### **Local and real-time payment schemes**


Local and real-time payment schemes enable **fast, low-cost domestic or regional bank transfers** without using international wire networks like SWIFT. These payments typically settle within seconds or hours and are commonly used for everyday transactions.


#### SEPA payments


SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) enables **euro transfers across participating European countries** . SEPA Credit Transfers and Direct Debits use IBAN as the primary identifier, and under the IBAN-only rule, a BIC is generally not required. SEPA payments are low-cost and typically settle instantly or within one business day.


#### Faster Payments (FPS)


Faster Payments is the UK’s real-time payment system for **domestic GBP transfers.** Payments typically settle within seconds and use a sort code and account number. It’s commonly used for everyday transfers between UK bank accounts.


## What is an IBAN (International Bank Account Number)?


An[IBAN](https://www.swift.com/standards/data-standards/iban-international-bank-account-number) **** helps **identify an individual bank account for cross-border payments** . It’s defined under the ISO 13616 standard, with SWIFT acting as the registration authority for IBAN formats.


### How long is an IBAN?


An IBAN is up to **34 alphanumeric characters** in total.


#### Standard IBAN structure


-


Two-letter country code


-


Two check digits (checksum)


-


And then a country-specific BBAN (Basic Bank Account Number) portion


### Why IBAN and BIC are often used together


When used together, **IBAN (account) + BIC (bank)** can support more **automated processing** and **fewer manual repairs** in cross-border payments.


#### Example: UK IBAN (structure)


**GB22MIDL12345612345678**


-


**GB** = country


-


**22** = check digits


-


**MIDL** = bank identifier (part of the BBAN structure in the UK format)


-


**123456** = sort code (UK domestic)


-


**12345678** = account number


## What is a routing number (ABA/RTN)?


If you’re **sending payments through the U.S. local payment network** (ACH, or Automated Clearing House), you’ll need the **recipient’s account number** and **9-digit ABA routing number** (ABA/RTN; American Bankers Association/Routing Transit Number).


### When are routing numbers required?


-


**ACH transfers** in the U.S. use routing transit numbers to route payments to the correct RDFI (receiving bank).


-


**Routing numbers** are also commonly used for **domestic wires** , though some banks use different routing numbers for wires vs. ACH (so you must confirm which one applies). This is a practical reality across many banks’ setups.


#### Example: What a routing number looks like


**123456789**


The structure of a routing number is typically described as:


-


1234 (Federal Reserve routing symbol)


-


5678 (ABA institution identifier)


-


9 (Check digit (used for validation))


### Where to find a routing number


The American Bankers Association (ABA) notes the routing number appears **on the bottom of checks** (left-most number), and **banks also publish it online** .


## How to avoid failed or delayed international payments


Before sending an international payment, it’s important to **verify all required details** .


### Your international payment checklist


-


**You’re using the right payment type** Wire vs. ACH vs. local transfer method can change which codes are required.


-


**The beneficiary name matches the account** Mismatches can trigger compliance checks or returns.


-


**IBAN length and format look valid (where applicable)** IBANs have defined country formats and check digits.


-


**You have the correct bank identifier** SWIFT/BIC for[cross-border](https://www.corpay.com/en-GB/cross-border) wires; routing (ABA/RTN) for U.S. ACH (and often wires).


-


**For SEPA euro payments, start with IBAN** IBAN-only has been standard since 2016 for SEPA euro transfers/direct debits.


## FAQs


**Is a SWIFT code the same as a BIC?**


Yes, in practice, SWIFT code and BIC are often used interchangeably. A BIC is the official standard, 8 characters, with an optional 3-character branch code (11 characters total).


**Do I always need both IBAN and SWIFT/BIC?**


Not always. Many international wire payments require both an IBAN (account) and a SWIFT/BIC (bank), but for SEPA euro payments, the IBAN-only rule usually applies.


**What if my supplier doesn’t have an IBAN?**


Some countries don’t use IBANs. In those cases, you’ll use the supplier’s local account details plus the required bank identifier (often a SWIFT/BIC for international wire payments).


**What is the difference between an IBAN and a SWIFT code?**


An IBAN identifies the beneficiary account number internationally, while a SWIFT code identifies the bank that holds that account.


**Can routing numbers be used for international transfers?**


Routing numbers are mainly used for U.S. domestic transactions (ACH and wires) and are not a substitute for SWIFT or IBAN in most cross-border payments.


**What happens if I enter an incorrect banking code?**


Incorrect codes can cause delayed payments, rejections, or returned funds. Always double-check beneficiary details before submitting.
